title: Casa Batlló or Casa Milà: which Gaudí house to enter if you only pay for one
subtitle: Two houses on the same avenue, a cheaper third near La Rambla, and ticket names that say little about what you get.
excerpt: Casa Batlló and Casa Milà stand five minutes apart in Barcelona and both are expensive. What you see inside each, who each one suits, why Palau Güell is the quiet third choice, and what the ticket tiers and the partner's listings really include.
longtail_phrases: is Casa Batlló or Casa Milà better
which Gaudí house is worth going inside
what is the difference between Casa Batlló tickets
is Palau Güell worth visiting
can you see Casa Batlló from outside for free
meta_title: Casa Batlló or Casa Milà: which Gaudí house to enter
meta_description: Casa Batlló, Casa Milà or Palau Güell: what you see inside each Gaudí house in Barcelona, who each suits, and what the ticket tiers really include.

featured_image.alt: The top of the front of Casa Batlló in Barcelona: a roof of coloured scales like an animal's back, and a small tower ending in a cross

content_html:
[place attraction="palau-guell" city="barcelona"]

While Casa Milà was going up, between 1906 and 1912, Barcelona laughed at it. People called it La Pedrera, the stone quarry, and the name stuck. The satirical papers drew it as a hangar for airships. The owners, Pere Milà and his wife Roser Segimon, had wanted the grandest apartment block on the Passeig de Gràcia. They got a building the city fined for breaking its rules, and a quarrel with their architect over his fees that ended in court. Antoni Gaudí won the case, and gave the money away.

It was the last house he built. After it he took no more private work and gave his time to the Sagrada Família, and when he died in 1926 Roser Segimon had her own flat redecorated in a more ordinary taste. A century later La Pedrera is on the UNESCO list, and so is Casa Batlló, which Gaudí had finished a few years earlier, five minutes down the same avenue. Both are among the dearest tickets in the city. Most visitors pay for one of them, and the question is which.

What you get without a ticket

The two fronts. Casa Batlló is at number 43 of the Passeig de Gràcia and Casa Milà at number 92, about 500 metres further up on the other side. Both face the pavement.

Casa Batlló was an ordinary block of 1877 that Gaudí rebuilt between 1904 and 1906 for Josep Batlló, a textile manufacturer. He covered the front in broken glass and ceramic discs, gave it balconies like masks and columns like bones, and arched the roof like the back of an animal. Barcelona reads it as the dragon killed by Saint George, with the small tower and its cross as the lance. Casa Milà was built from the ground up: a cliff of pale limestone in waves, with balconies of twisted iron.

Casa Milà from the far pavement. The front is free to look at, and it is half the visit. Photo: Yair Haklai, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Inside Casa Batlló

The visit climbs through one family's home. You see the main floor, with its great window over the avenue and its doors of carved oak. You pass the light well, lined with blue tiles that are darker at the top and paler at the bottom, so that the light looks even all the way down. Under the roof is a loft of white arches, and above it the terrace with the dragon's back and the chimneys.

The house is small and very busy, and in the middle of the day you move at the speed of the people in front. An audio guide is part of the visit, and in recent years rooms of projected light and sound have been added at the start and the end. Allow an hour, or a little more.

The light well of Casa Batlló: the tiles are darker at the top and paler at the bottom. Photo: FrancoisLagunas, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

Inside Casa Milà

Here you visit a building more than a home. You enter through one of the two courtyards, open to the sky, and go straight up to the roof: a rolling terrace of stair heads, ventilation towers and chimneys grouped like helmeted guards. Below it, the attic is a long tunnel of some 270 brick arches, with models that show how Gaudí worked out his structures. One apartment is furnished as a well-off family would have had it around 1910. A few tenants still live in the building.

Allow an hour and a quarter. The roof is the high point, and in wet weather it can be closed for safety, so look at the forecast before you fix a day.

The chimneys on the roof of Casa Milà, grouped like helmeted guards. Photo: José Luiz, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

Which one to choose

  • Casa Batlló if you want colour and invention in every door handle, and do not mind a crowd. It is usually the dearer of the two.
  • Casa Milà if you want the roof, and want to understand how Gaudí built. It has more space and more explanation.
  • Palau Güell if the price of the other two puts you off, or if you want a Gaudí interior almost to yourself.

Palau Güell, the third choice

Gaudí built this town house between 1886 and 1890 for Eusebi Güell, the industrialist who became his patron. It stands in a narrow street a few steps off La Rambla. It is an early work, dark and serious. The stables in the basement rest on brick pillars shaped like mushrooms. The central hall rises through the whole house to a dome pierced with small holes, which let in daylight like stars. On the roof are twenty chimneys, most of them clad in broken tile.

It belongs to the provincial government, costs a fraction of the other two, and seldom has much of a line.

One of the twenty chimneys on the roof of Palau Güell, clad in broken tile. Photo: Fred Romero, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

What the ticket names mean

  • Casa Batlló tiers. The house sells its visit in levels named after colours and metals, and the names have changed more than once. The pattern stays: the cheapest level is the house with an audio guide, and the dearer ones add extra rooms, priority at the door or the right to change your date. Read the list of what is included, not the name.
  • Early entrance lets you in before the general opening. In a house this crowded, that is worth more than most extras.
  • Casa Milà sells a daytime visit, and separately an evening one with projections on the roof. They are different products.

On our partner's listings, the Casa Batlló ticket marked as all-inclusive describes access to every area, priority entry and the rooms of light and sound. The early entrance listing says very little, so check what it names before you pay. For Casa Milà there is a plain entrance ticket, and one sold with an audio guide in the partner's app. Bring earphones. The Güell Palace ticket comes with an audio walk through the old town: the commentary is for the streets, not for the inside of the palace. The Gaudí Experience is not a Gaudí building. It is a small exhibition with a film, near Park Güell.

These are the tickets our partner sells for the Gaudí houses, with today's prices:

[partner city="barcelona" match="casa,batllo,mila,pedrera,guell,gaudi" limit="6"]

When to go

Both houses on the avenue sell entry for a set time, and the good hours go first. Take the first slot of the morning or one late in the afternoon. For Casa Batlló the nearest metro station is Passeig de Gràcia, and for Casa Milà it is Diagonal. Opening hours for Palau Güell change with the season and are on our page for Palau Güell.

From here

Next door to Casa Batlló stands Casa Amatller, by another architect of the same years, and the pair show why this stretch is called the Block of Discord. Up in the Gràcia quarter, Casa Vicens is the first house Gaudí built. Park Güell is a bus ride further up the hill, and the Sagrada Família is two metro stops from Diagonal. See what else there is in Barcelona, or open the trip planner for Spain.

Cover photo: Bernard Gagnon, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

faqs.q: Is Casa Batlló or Casa Milà better?
faqs.a: Casa Batlló is the more colourful and inventive interior, and the more crowded. Casa Milà has the better roof and explains more about how Gaudí built. If you want one, choose by which of those matters more to you.

faqs.q: Can you see Casa Batlló and Casa Milà without a ticket?
faqs.a: Yes, from outside. Both fronts face the pavement of the Passeig de Gràcia, about 500 metres apart, and looking at them is free.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the Casa Batlló tickets?
faqs.a: The house sells the same visit in levels. The cheapest is the house with an audio guide, and the dearer ones add extra rooms, priority entry or the right to change the date. The names have changed over the years, so read what is included.

faqs.q: Is Palau Güell worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, if you want a Gaudí interior without the crowd or the price of the two houses on the Passeig de Gràcia. It is an early, darker work, with a domed central hall and a roof of tiled chimneys.

faqs.q: How long does a visit to Casa Batlló or Casa Milà take?
faqs.a: About an hour for Casa Batlló and an hour and a quarter for Casa Milà. Both sell entry for a set time, so book the slot in advance.

title: Royal Palace of Madrid or the Royal Collections Gallery: which to enter, and what each ticket includes
subtitle: Two buildings on the same esplanade, one owner, two separate tickets, and a good deal around them that is free.
excerpt: The Royal Palace of Madrid and the Royal Collections Gallery stand side by side and are sold separately. What each visit is like, which one suits you, what is free around them, and what the partner's tickets and audio tours include.
focus_keyword: Royal Palace of Madrid or Royal Collections Gallery
secondary_keywords: what does the Royal Palace ticket include
longtail_phrases: is the Royal Collections Gallery worth visiting
is the Royal Palace of Madrid worth it
what does the Royal Palace of Madrid ticket include
are the gardens of the Royal Palace of Madrid free
how long does the Royal Palace of Madrid take
meta_title: Royal Palace of Madrid or Royal Collections Gallery
meta_description: The Royal Palace of Madrid or the Royal Collections Gallery next door: what each visit is like, which to choose, what is free and what tickets include.

featured_image.alt: The long stone south front of the Royal Palace of Madrid across the empty paving of the Plaza de la Armería at dusk

content_html:
[place attraction="royal-palace-of-madrid" city="madrid"]

On Christmas Eve 1734 a fire started in the old Alcázar of Madrid, the fortress palace where the kings of Spain had lived for generations. It burned for four days. More than five hundred paintings were lost. Others were cut from their frames and thrown from the windows, and one of those saved that night was Las Meninas, by Velázquez.

Philip V, the first Bourbon king of Spain, had grown up at Versailles and had never liked the Alcázar. He ordered a new palace on the same spot, built of stone and brick with vaulted ceilings in place of timber, so that it could not burn again. The Italian architect Filippo Juvarra drew it and died within two years. His pupil Giovanni Battista Sacchetti built it from 1738, and Charles III moved in in 1764. In 2023 a second building opened beside it, a museum for what the kings collected. The two are run by the same public body and sold with separate tickets, and most visitors have time for one.

Two buildings on one esplanade

The palace stands on the edge of a bluff above the river Manzanares. Its south front looks across a parade ground, the Plaza de la Armería, to the Almudena Cathedral. The Royal Collections Gallery is next to the cathedral, built down the slope, so that from the top you see only a long pale wall and the visit descends floor by floor. Both entrances are within three minutes' walk of each other.

What the palace visit is

The palace has more than three thousand rooms, and the king does not live in any of them: the royal family's home is outside the city, and this building is used for state ceremonies. The public route is one way, through about two dozen rooms on the main floor. It takes an hour and a half.

  • The main staircase, wide and shallow, under a painted vault.
  • The Throne Room, hung with red velvet, with the ceiling Giambattista Tiepolo finished in 1764, when he was nearly seventy.
  • The Gasparini Room, where the king dressed, covered from floor to ceiling in embroidered silk and stucco.
  • The Porcelain Room, whose walls are plaques made at the royal factory.
  • The Royal Chapel and a room of instruments made by Stradivari.
  • The Royal Armoury, across the courtyard, with the armour of Charles V.

The Royal Kitchen, in the basement, is a separate visit with its own ticket. Because the palace is in use, it closes for official events, sometimes at short notice.

The main staircase, where the visit begins. Photo: José Luis Filpo Cabana, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.

The Throne Room, hung with red velvet under the ceiling Tiepolo painted in the 1760s. Photo: José Luis Filpo Cabana, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.

What the gallery is

The Royal Collections Gallery took about twenty-five years to plan and build, to a design by Emilio Tuñón and Luis Mansilla. It is a museum in the modern sense: wide, cool rooms, labels in two languages, benches, lifts. The floors go down in order of time. First come the Habsburg kings, then the Bourbons, then a floor for temporary exhibitions.

What is on show was chosen from the royal palaces and convents around Spain: paintings by Velázquez, Caravaggio and Goya, huge Flemish tapestries, armour, state carriages. Part of the display is changed from time to time. During the building work a stretch of the ninth-century wall of Muslim Madrid was found, and it has been left where it was, inside the museum. Allow an hour and a half.

The Royal Collections Gallery, set into the slope below the cathedral. Photo: Javier Perez Montes, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Which one to enter

  • The palace if this is your first time in Madrid and you want the rooms themselves: the ceilings, the silk, the sense of a court.
  • The gallery if you have already walked through a royal palace somewhere else and would sooner look closely at fewer things, with an explanation beside each.
  • The gallery also on a very hot or wet afternoon, or when the line at the palace runs along the railings.
  • Both fit in one day: the palace when it opens, lunch, then the gallery. Do not add the Prado to the same day.

What is free around them

  • Plaza de Oriente, the square on the east side, with its row of stone kings, carved for the roofline of the palace and left at ground level.
  • The Sabatini Gardens, on the north side: clipped hedges, a pool and the best full view of a palace front.
  • The Campo del Moro, the park below the west front. It is public, but its gate is at the bottom of the hill, on the river side, so it is a walk of a quarter of an hour from the palace door.
  • The Almudena Cathedral, begun in 1883 and consecrated only in 1993. Its museum and dome have a ticket.
  • The changing of the guard, held at the palace gates on certain days of the week.

For citizens of the European Union and of Latin American countries, the palace has long had free entry in the last two hours of some weekdays, with identification and a long line. Check that it still applies before you plan around it.

The palace from the Campo del Moro, the public park below its west front. Photo: Benjamín Núñez González, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What the partner's listings include

  • The Royal Palace ticket is entry to the palace by the fast-track door. The listing says the Royal Kitchen is not included.
  • The palace ticket with an audio tour adds commentary in the partner's app, with a route from room to room. Bring earphones.
  • The palace audio tour "without a ticket" is the same commentary alone. You buy entry yourself.
  • The Royal Collections Gallery ticket is entry to the gallery and its temporary exhibition. The "digital royal guide" sold with it is, by its description, a text to read on your phone, not an audio tour of the rooms.
  • The Royal Palace of Aranjuez is a different palace, in a town about 45 kilometres south of Madrid, reached by commuter train. Do not buy it by mistake.
  • The audio walks of royal Madrid are for the streets and squares. Tickets on the way are not included.

These are the tickets and audio tours our partner sells for the palace and the gallery, with today's prices:

[partner city="madrid" match="royal,palace,collections" limit="6"]

Getting there, and when

The nearest metro station is Ópera, five minutes away on foot. Go at opening time: by late morning the tour groups fill the staircase. Bags are scanned at both doors. Hours change between summer and winter and are on our page for the Royal Palace of Madrid.

From here

The Plaza Mayor is ten minutes east on foot, and the Temple of Debod, an Egyptian temple rebuilt in a park to the north, is the place for the sunset. See our pages for the Royal Collections Gallery, the Almudena Cathedral and the Plaza de Oriente, look at the rest of Madrid, or open the trip planner for Spain.

Cover photo: Javier Perez Montes, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Is the Royal Collections Gallery worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, if you like to look closely at paintings, tapestries, armour and carriages with an explanation beside each. It is calmer and cooler than the palace and takes about an hour and a half.

faqs.q: Should you visit the Royal Palace of Madrid or the Royal Collections Gallery?
faqs.a: On a first visit to Madrid, the palace, for the rooms themselves. If you have seen other royal palaces, or the line is long, the gallery. Both fit in one day if you start at opening time.

faqs.q: What does the Royal Palace of Madrid ticket include?
faqs.a: The one-way route through the state rooms, the Royal Chapel and the Royal Armoury. The Royal Kitchen is a separate visit with its own ticket.

faqs.q: Are the gardens of the Royal Palace of Madrid free?
faqs.a: Yes. The Sabatini Gardens and the Campo del Moro are public parks with their own gates. The gate of the Campo del Moro is at the bottom of the hill, on the river side.

faqs.q: How long does the Royal Palace of Madrid take?
faqs.a: About an hour and a half for the public route, a little more with the Royal Armoury. The palace can close for official events at short notice.

title: Picasso in Málaga: the museum or the birthplace, and the walk on to the Alcazaba
subtitle: Two Picasso museums five minutes apart, a Roman theatre and a Moorish fortress at the end of the same street.
excerpt: Málaga has two Picasso museums: the Museo Picasso and the house where he was born. What each one shows, which to choose, how to walk from one to the other and on to the Roman theatre, the Alcazaba and Gibralfaro, and what the partner sells.
focus_keyword: Museo Picasso Málaga or Picasso birthplace
longtail_phrases: which Picasso museum in Málaga is better
is the Picasso birthplace museum worth visiting
how long does the Museo Picasso Málaga take
can you walk from the Alcazaba to Gibralfaro
is the Roman theatre in Málaga free
meta_title: Picasso in Málaga: the museum or the birthplace
meta_description: The Museo Picasso or the house where he was born: what each shows, which to choose, and the short walk on to the Roman theatre and the Alcazaba.

featured_image.alt: The stone tiers of the Roman theatre of Málaga at the foot of the hill, with the walls and towers of the Alcazaba above

content_html:
[place attraction="museo-picasso-malaga" city="malaga"]

Pablo Ruiz Picasso was born in Málaga on 25 October 1881, in a rented flat on the Plaza de la Merced. His father, José Ruiz Blasco, taught drawing, looked after the town's small museum, and painted pigeons, which he kept as models and which his son drew before he could write. In 1891 the father took a teaching post in A Coruña, at the other end of Spain, and the family left. The boy was nine.

He came back for a few holidays as a young man, the last of them around 1900, and then never again. He lived in France, and after the Civil War he refused to return to Spain while Franco ruled. He died in 1973, two years before the dictator. He had wanted his work to be shown in the town where he was born, and in 2003 that happened, when a museum opened with works given by his daughter-in-law Christine and his grandson Bernard. So Málaga has two Picasso places, five minutes apart on foot, and visitors with one morning ask which to enter.

The Museo Picasso Málaga

The museum is in the Buenavista Palace, a sixteenth-century house with an arcaded courtyard and carved wooden ceilings, in a lane near the cathedral. It holds more than two hundred works, and they cover his whole life: a boy's careful studies, portraits of his first wife Olga and of his son, Cubist heads, ceramics, sculpture, and the loose late paintings of the 1970s.

Two things are worth knowing in advance. This is a family collection, so it is strong on what Picasso kept for himself and has few of the pictures printed in every book. Guernica is in Madrid. And the hanging is changed every few years, with temporary exhibitions alongside. In the basement you can see what the builders found: stretches of the Phoenician town wall and Roman vats for salting fish.

Allow an hour and a half. Entry is for a set time, and the museum has its own audio guide.

The courtyard of the Buenavista Palace, which houses the Museo Picasso. Photo: Emilio Luque, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The birthplace

The house on the Plaza de la Merced was built in 1861 and has been a protected monument since 1983. The museum fills the first floor, where the family lived. It is a small visit about a childhood, with a room furnished as in the 1880s, family papers and photographs, paintings by the father, and prints, ceramics and illustrated books by the son. A second room on the same square is used for temporary shows.

Allow half an hour to three quarters. It is one of the cheapest tickets in the city.

The row of houses on the Plaza de la Merced where Picasso was born in 1881. Photo: Palickap, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Which one to choose

  • The Museo Picasso if you want to look at art. It is the only one of the two with a real run of paintings.
  • The birthplace if you have little time or money, or if you already know the work and are curious about where it began.
  • Both fit in a morning, and they do not repeat each other. Start at the birthplace: the story then runs in the right order.

The walk between them, and on

The whole route is about 600 metres, flat, and closed to cars for most of its length.

  • Plaza de la Merced. The birthplace is in the row of houses on the north side. A bronze Picasso sits on a bench under the trees, and the obelisk in the middle marks the grave of General Torrijos and his companions, shot on a beach near here in 1831 for rising against the king.
  • Calle Granada. Two minutes down this street is the church of Santiago, with a brick tower in the Mudéjar style. Picasso was baptised here.
  • Calle San Agustín. This side street leads to the Museo Picasso.
  • Calle Alcazabilla. One block east, the street opens on to the Roman theatre, built in the time of Augustus and lost until 1951, when building work uncovered it. You see all of it from the pavement, for nothing.
  • The Alcazaba. Its gate is beside the theatre.

The Alcazaba and Gibralfaro

The Alcazaba is the palace and fortress of the Muslim rulers of Málaga, built mostly in the eleventh century on the slope above the port. You climb through a double line of walls, by gates set at angles to slow an attacker and held up in places by Roman columns taken from the theatre below. At the top are small courts with pools, horseshoe arches and gardens. It takes an hour, and tickets are sold at the entrance.

Higher up the same hill is the castle of Gibralfaro, of the fourteenth century, with the widest view of the port, the bullring and the coast. A walled passage joins the two, but it is not open: from the Alcazaba you go back out and climb a steep path of twenty minutes, or take a city bus. A combined ticket has usually been on sale, and Sunday afternoons have long been free at both. Check before you count on either.

One of the garden courts inside the Alcazaba. Photo: Diego Delso, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The port and the bullring from Gibralfaro, the castle above the Alcazaba. Photo: Daniel Capilla, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What the partner's listings include

  • Museo Picasso entry with a city walk: the museum ticket and an audio walk through the old town in the partner's app. The listing says there is no commentary inside the museum.
  • Museo Picasso entry ticket: the ticket alone. Its list of inclusions mentions a live guide, which the title does not. Do not count on one unless the listing confirms it when you book.
  • Picasso Birthplace Museum: an entry ticket.
  • The Alcazaba audio tour: commentary only, on your own phone. The listing says entry is bought at the gate.
  • Two audio walks of the old town, which pass the theatre, the cathedral and both Picasso museums. Tickets on the way are not included. Bring earphones.

These are the Picasso tickets and the audio walks our partner sells in Málaga, with today's prices:

[partner city="malaga" match="picasso,alcazaba,old" limit="6"]

When to go

In summer, climb the Alcazaba as soon as it opens or in the last hour, and keep the museums for the middle of the day. The streets around the Plaza de la Merced are at their best in the evening. Opening hours are on our pages for the Museo Picasso Málaga and the Alcazaba.

From here

The cathedral, two minutes from the Museo Picasso, is known as the one-armed lady, because its second tower was never built. Beyond it the old port has been turned into a promenade. See our pages for the birthplace and the castle of Gibralfaro, look at the rest of Málaga, or open the trip planner for Spain.

Cover photo: Benjamin Smith, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Which Picasso museum in Málaga is better?
faqs.a: For art, the Museo Picasso Málaga, with more than two hundred works from his whole life. The birthplace is a small visit about his childhood and family. They are five minutes apart and do not repeat each other.

faqs.q: Is the Picasso birthplace museum worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, as a short and cheap visit of half an hour to three quarters. It shows the flat where the family lived, his father's paintings and some of his prints and ceramics, not major canvases.

faqs.q: How long does the Museo Picasso Málaga take?
faqs.a: About an hour and a half, including the archaeological remains in the basement. Entry is for a set time.

faqs.q: Is the Roman theatre in Málaga free?
faqs.a: You see the whole theatre from the pavement of Calle Alcazabilla without paying. It lies at the foot of the Alcazaba, beside its gate.

faqs.q: Can you walk from the Alcazaba to Gibralfaro?
faqs.a: Not from inside. You leave the Alcazaba and climb a steep path of about twenty minutes outside the walls, or take a city bus to the castle.

title: Belém in Lisbon: what is free at Jerónimos, what needs a ticket, and how to get there

featured_image.alt: The long carved limestone south front of the Jerónimos Monastery in Lisbon, with its domed tower, under a blue sky

content_html:
[place attraction="jeronimos-monastery" city="lisbon"]

On the night of 7 July 1497 Vasco da Gama and his crews are said to have prayed until morning in a small chapel on the beach at Restelo, a few kilometres down the river from Lisbon. Prince Henry the Navigator had founded it for sailors. The next day four ships left for India by a route no European had sailed, and two years later two of them came back.

King Manuel I had a monastery built where the chapel stood, from about 1501, and paid for it with a tax of one twentieth on the spices that now came round Africa. He gave it to the monks of Saint Jerome, whose duty was to pray for the king and to hear the confessions of men about to sail. The work took most of a century. Today its south front runs for nearly three hundred metres along a garden, and on most mornings two lines of people stand in front of it. They lead to different doors, and only one of them needs a ticket.

Two doors, two lines

The two entrances are close together, at the west end of the church. One is for the church, and it is free. The other is for the cloister, and it needs a ticket. The great carved doorway in the middle of the south front, which everyone photographs, is not the way in.

Ask which line you are in before you join it. People wait a long time for the cloister when they wanted the church, and the other way round.

The church: free

The church of Santa Maria de Belém is one tall hall. Six carved columns, thin as tree trunks, rise about twenty-five metres and spread into a single vault with no walls between nave and aisles. Just inside the door, on either side, are the tombs of Vasco da Gama and of the poet Luís de Camões, who wrote the epic of the voyage. Both were carved in the nineteenth century. At the far end, the tombs of King Manuel and his family rest on marble elephants.

Visitors are not let in during services, and shoulders should be covered. Twenty minutes are enough.

The church: slender carved columns under a single vault. This part is free. Photo: Schwarze engel, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

The tomb of Vasco da Gama, just inside the church door. Photo: Jakub Hałun, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

The cloister: ticket

The cloister is why people pay. It has two storeys, square, in honey-coloured limestone. Its builders, Diogo de Boitaca and after him João de Castilho, covered every arch and pillar with carving in the style named after King Manuel: ropes, leaves, armillary spheres, the cross of the Order of Christ. The same ticket takes you into the old refectory, lined with tile panels, and into the chapter house. It also lets you into the upper choir, from which you look down the length of the church. The poet Fernando Pessoa has been buried in the cloister since 1985.

Allow an hour. Buy the ticket before you come: sales at the monastery itself have been limited in recent years, and holders of a ticket still wait in the line for the door. The monastery has long been closed on Mondays.

A gallery of the cloister. This is the part behind the ticket. Photo: Bex Walton, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

What else in Belém is free, and what is not

  • Free: the garden in front of the monastery, the walk along the river, and the outside of every monument. In the paving at the foot of the Monument of the Discoveries there is a map of the world in coloured marble, with the dates of the Portuguese voyages.
  • The Monument of the Discoveries was raised in 1960, five hundred years after the death of Prince Henry, who stands at its prow. A lift to the terrace on top has a ticket.
  • The Belém Tower was built between 1514 and 1520 to guard the mouth of the river. Inside there is a narrow spiral stair and a few bare rooms, and the line to enter has always been long for what you see. The tower was closed for conservation work in 2025. Check on our page whether it has reopened. The outside, from the shore, is the main thing in any case.
  • The museums each have their own ticket: the Coach Museum near the station, the Maritime Museum in the west wing of the monastery building, and the art and technology museums on the riverbank.
  • The custard tarts. The bakery a few doors east of the monastery has made them since 1837. The line on the pavement is for the takeaway counter. The wait for a table inside is often shorter.

The figures on the Monument of the Discoveries, raised on the riverbank in 1960. Photo: Jakub Hałun, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

How to get there

  • Tram 15 runs from Praça da Figueira and Praça do Comércio and stops in front of the monastery. It takes about half an hour, it is crowded, and it is a favourite of pickpockets.
  • The train on the Cascais line leaves from Cais do Sodré and reaches Belém station in under ten minutes. Take a stopping train, since the fast ones do not call there. From the station it is ten minutes on foot to the monastery.

A railway and a main road run between the monastery and the river. You cross them by the underpass at the Monument of the Discoveries, or by footbridges near the station and near the tower. From the monument, the tower is a quarter of an hour's walk west along the water.

The Belém Tower from the shore, which is how most people see it. Photo: Berthold Werner, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What the partner's listings include

  • The Jerónimos Monastery ticket is entry to the cloister and the refectory. The listing says plainly that it is not a fast track, and that the archaeology museum in the same building is not part of it.
  • The ticket with an audio tour adds commentary in the partner's app, for the church and the cloister.
  • The audio tour alone has no ticket. It is enough if you only want the church.
  • Two audio walks through Belém are for the outdoors, from the monastery to the monument and the tower. Entry to anything on the way is not included. Bring earphones.

A half day in order

Arrive a little before opening and do the cloister first, then the church. Have the tart, cross by the underpass to the monument, and walk along the river to the tower. From there a tram or bus runs back to the centre from the street behind. Current hours are on our page for the Jerónimos Monastery.

From here

Sintra and the coast at Cascais are for another day, and the train to Cascais passes through Belém. See our pages for the Belém Tower, the Monument of the Discoveries and the National Coach Museum, look at the rest of Lisbon, or open the trip planner for Portugal.

Cover photo: Dennis G. Jarvis, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

faqs.q: Is the Jerónimos Monastery free to enter?
faqs.a: The church is free. The cloister, the refectory and the upper choir need a ticket. The two have separate doors and separate lines, close together at the west end of the church.

faqs.q: Where are the tombs of Vasco da Gama and Camões?
faqs.a: In the church, just inside the door, on either side. You do not need a ticket to see them.

faqs.q: How do you get to Belém from the centre of Lisbon?
faqs.a: By tram 15 from Praça da Figueira or Praça do Comércio, in about half an hour, or by a stopping train on the Cascais line from Cais do Sodré, in under ten minutes, then ten minutes on foot.

faqs.q: Is it worth going inside the Belém Tower?
faqs.a: The outside is the main sight. Inside there is a narrow spiral stair and a few bare rooms. The tower was closed for conservation work in 2025, so check whether it has reopened.

faqs.q: How long do you need in Belém?
faqs.a: Half a day: about an hour and a half for the cloister and the church, then the walk by the river to the Monument of the Discoveries and the tower. Add an hour for each museum.

featured_image.alt: The towers and palaces of the Alhambra on their wooded hill in evening light, with the snow of the Sierra Nevada behind

content_html:
[place attraction="alhambra-es" city="granada"]

On 2 January 1492 the last Muslim ruler in Spain, the emir the Spaniards called Boabdil, gave up Granada to Ferdinand and Isabella, and his family's palace on the hill became a royal possession. For a time it was cared for. Then the court lost interest, the halls were left to squatters, and in 1812 French troops, leaving the fortress they had occupied, blew up several of its towers.

In 1829 an American writer, Washington Irving, was allowed to lodge in the empty royal rooms for a few months. His Tales of the Alhambra, published in 1832, sent travellers to Granada, and the travellers shamed the state into repairs that have gone on ever since. The Alhambra is now among the most visited monuments in Spain, and entry is rationed. That is the reason for the complicated tickets, and for the one mistake that spoils most bad visits: buying a ticket that does not include the palaces.

Four parts, one of them timed

  • The Alcazaba: the fortress at the tip of the hill, and the oldest part. You climb the Torre de la Vela for the view over the city.
  • The Nasrid Palaces: the rooms and courts of the emirs, built mostly in the fourteenth century. Here are the Court of the Myrtles with its long pool, the Hall of the Ambassadors, and the Court of the Lions with its fountain on twelve stone lions. This is what the Alhambra is famous for.
  • The Partal and the gardens along the walls.
  • The Generalife: the emirs' summer estate on the next slope, with its water court and terraced gardens.

All four are behind ticket checks. Only the Nasrid Palaces have a time.

The Court of the Lions, in the Nasrid Palaces: the part with the timed entry. Photo: Benjamin Smith, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What "general" covers, and what it may not

At the monument's own ticket office, the general ticket covers all four parts, with a half-hour entry time for the Nasrid Palaces printed on it. A cheaper ticket covers the gardens, the Generalife and the Alcazaba, and leaves the palaces out. There are also night visits, to the palaces or to the gardens, sold separately.

Resellers use the same words more loosely. A page headed "general admission" or "Alhambra ticket" may be the ticket without the palaces. Two tests settle it. Does the list of what is included name the Nasrid Palaces? And are you given, or asked to choose, an entry time for them? If either answer is no, assume the palaces are not in it.

How the timed entry works

  • The time is for one door. It applies to the entrance of the Nasrid Palaces and to nothing else. You see the other parts before or after, on the same day.
  • Miss it and it is gone. Staff do not let latecomers in, and there is no second entry. Be in the line a quarter of an hour early.
  • The palaces are far from the main entrance. From the ticket pavilion at the top of the hill to their door is a walk of fifteen to twenty minutes. If your time is early, come in by the Gate of Justice instead, which is much closer.
  • Tickets carry your name. Bring the passport or identity card you booked with. It is checked at more than one point.
  • They sell out. In spring and autumn the palaces are booked weeks ahead.

With a morning slot, see the palaces first, then the Alcazaba, then the Generalife. Allow three hours at least.

The Alcazaba, the oldest part of the Alhambra, with the bell of the Torre de la Vela. Photo: Jebulon, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

The water court of the Generalife, the summer estate on the next hill. Photo: Benjamin Smith, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What is free on the hill

More than most people expect. From Plaza Nueva you walk up the Cuesta de Gomérez, through the Gate of the Pomegranates, and into a wood planted in the nineteenth century. The Gate of Justice, of 1348, is open to everyone. So is the Palace of Charles V, the Renaissance block with a circular courtyard that the emperor began in 1527 in the middle of the Moorish palaces. The Alhambra Museum on its ground floor has not charged for entry. You can also walk the street beside it, as far as the checkpoints.

What the partner's listings include

  • The Alhambra ticket with an audio tour lists entry to the Alcazaba, the Generalife, the Palace of Charles V, the Partal and the Alhambra Museum, with commentary in the partner's app. It states that the Nasrid Palaces are not included.
  • The Alhambra general admission ticket lists only "entrance ticket to Alhambra", and its description speaks of the Alcazaba and the Generalife. Apply the two tests above before you pay.
  • The audio tour "without a ticket" and the audio walk down into the old city are commentary alone.
  • The Sacromonte Caves Museum and the Palacio de los Olvidados are entry tickets for two small museums across the valley.

If the Nasrid Palaces are what you came for, buy a ticket that names them, with a time. The partner's tickets suit a visit to the gardens and the fortress, or a day when the palaces are sold out.

[partner city="granada" match="alhambra,general,admission,ticket,audio" limit="6"]

The afternoon: the Albaicín

The hill facing the Alhambra is the old Muslim town, on the UNESCO list since 1994: white houses, walled gardens and lanes too narrow for cars. Start at the bottom, on the Carrera del Darro, the street along the stream under the walls of the Alhambra. Near its start is a bathhouse of the eleventh century, with a small ticket. Then climb to the Mirador de San Nicolás, the terrace from which the Alhambra is photographed, with the Sierra Nevada behind it. It is full at sunset, and bags need watching. A minibus runs up from Plaza Nueva.

The Palacio de los Olvidados is in these lanes. According to the partner's listing it shows instruments of torture from the time of the Inquisition, and has a roof terrace facing the Alhambra.

The Albaicín from the Alhambra. The walk for the afternoon is over there. Photo: Ввласенко, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

Sacromonte

Beyond the Albaicín the road follows the valley into Sacromonte, where the houses are caves cut into the soft hillside. This has been the quarter of Granada's Roma families for centuries, and of their flamenco, which is still performed in the caves at night. The Caves Museum stands at the top of a steep path: a group of caves furnished as homes, a stable and workshops, with the Alhambra across the valley.

The front of a cave house in Sacromonte. The rooms run back into the hill. Photo: Jocelyn Erskine-Kellie, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

From here

In the lower town, the Royal Chapel holds the tombs of Ferdinand and Isabella, beside the cathedral. See our pages for the Alhambra, the Nasrid Palaces, the Mirador de San Nicolás and the Sacromonte Caves Museum, look at the rest of Granada, or open the trip planner for Spain.

Cover photo: Benjamin Smith and Diego Delso, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: What does the Alhambra general ticket include?
faqs.a: At the monument's own ticket office it covers the Alcazaba, the Nasrid Palaces at a set time, the Partal and the Generalife. Resellers sometimes use the same name for a ticket without the palaces, so check that the Nasrid Palaces are named.

faqs.q: What happens if you miss your Nasrid Palaces time?
faqs.a: You lose that part of the visit. Latecomers are not let in and there is no second entry, so be in the line a quarter of an hour before the time on the ticket.

faqs.q: Is the Alhambra worth visiting without the Nasrid Palaces?
faqs.a: The Alcazaba, the gardens and the Generalife fill two pleasant hours, but the palaces are what the Alhambra is famous for. If you can get a ticket that includes them, do.

faqs.q: What parts of the Alhambra are free?
faqs.a: The walk up through the wood, the Gate of Justice, the courtyard of the Palace of Charles V and the street between it and the church are open without a ticket.

faqs.q: What can you do in Granada after the Alhambra?
faqs.a: Walk the Carrera del Darro, climb through the Albaicín to the Mirador de San Nicolás for the view back to the Alhambra, and go on to the cave houses of Sacromonte.
